description: Labelled agent tools for measuring the local source classifier. Every module is parsed, never imported or executed. Labels describe what the tool does when called, never what it is named.

label_definitions.read: Only reads: local reads, pure computation, SELECT-shaped queries.
label_definitions.sensitive: Reads credentials or secrets, or executes arbitrary code or processes.
label_definitions.undecidable: Behaviour is chosen at runtime, or the implementation is absent.

cases.rationale: Name claims a local config read, but the body issues rq.post(...) to an internal HTTP endpoint through an aliased requests import. Network egress dominates; nothing local is opened. Tests name-vs-behaviour and `import requests as rq` alias resolution.

The FastMCP tool body contains no network call itself; the httpx.Client is constructed in the module-level helper _fetch, bound to a local, entered as a context manager, and .get() is called on the with-target rather than the original name. Requires interprocedural reach plus receiver tracking through `with ... as`.

Async FastMCP tool performing an HTTP GET via an aliased aiohttp ClientSession inside nested async-with blocks. Purely read-shaped output (a list of titles) but the read crosses the network, so external outranks read. Tests async function bodies and aliased third-party client imports.

MCP @server.call_tool() handler builds an EmailMessage (pure stdlib formatting) and hands it to the _deliver helper, which opens an smtplib.SMTP connection, STARTTLS, and sends. No credential material is read and no local state changes, so the class is external rather than sensitive or write. The only egress is one call level down from the tool.

Tool is a class method registered via @kernel_function. A raw TCP socket is opened, connected, written to and read from — but only on the else path: the dry_run branch returns a formatted string with no egress. Since the network branch is reachable, the tool is external. Tests `from socket import socket as Sock` aliasing, effects inside a branch, and effects reached only through a class method.

Registered through StructuredTool.from_function. head_object on a boto3 S3 client is an AWS API call over the network. It is read-only against the bucket and touches no credential file in this source, so external is the class (boto3's implicit credential resolution is not visible here and does not make it sensitive).

An @mcp.tool()-decorated method on a class. The model client is built in __init__ under an aliased import (`from openai import OpenAI as Client`), stored on self, then re-bound to a local (`chat = self._client.chat.completions`) before .create() is called. Egress is an inference API call. Tests attribute-held receivers, partial-chain locals, and aliased SDK constructors.

Plain function discovered only by its appearance in tools=[...] on an agent constructor. The body constructs an Anthropic client into a local named `handle` and calls messages.create, an outbound model API request. Nothing is written locally and no secret is read in-source, so external.

MCP @server.call_tool() async handler. `from requests import Session as S` hides the library name entirely; the session object lives in a local, is mutated, then used for a GET against a remote CRM API. Read-shaped semantics but the read is remote, so external.

Second name-contradiction case: the name and description both say local log grepping, and the tool body only calls a helper. The helper builds a urllib.request.Request with a JSON body and calls urlopen against a remote Elasticsearch endpoint — an HTTP POST via stdlib rather than a recognisable HTTP library. Tests stdlib-only egress plus interprocedural reach through StructuredTool.from_function registration.

Precedence probe: the tool genuinely writes durable state (mkdir plus Path.write_text) and then also POSTs to a remote ingest endpoint. Both write and external apply, and external outranks write, so the correct label is external. A classifier that stops at the first effect it recognises will label this write.

Plain function reachable only via tools=[...] passed to ReActAgent.from_tools. The early-return branch does pure string formatting; the default path opens an ftplib.FTP connection, logs in anonymously, and retrbinary's a remote file into an in-memory buffer. FTP is a less-common egress channel than HTTP, and the effect sits behind a default-True flag guard. The io.BytesIO write is in-process only, so external, not write.

FastMCP @mcp.tool(). The name promises deletion, but the body only opens the ledger for reading through the _load_rows helper, filters in memory, and returns a formatted string. No open() in a write mode, no network, no secrets, no process launch -> read. Tests that the classifier ignores the verb 'purge' in the name.

Async FastMCP tool. Named 'local_price_cache' and documented as returning cached prices, but the await chain goes tool -> _gather -> aiohttp.ClientSession (imported aliased as ah) -> session.get on an https endpoint. Outbound HTTP two helper hops away and behind an alias -> external.

Low-level MCP @server.call_tool() with literal string branch dispatch. The 'inspect_note' branch only reads, but the 'mark_reviewed' branch calls _stamp, which opens the target in append mode and writes. Both branches are statically visible literals, so the handler is decidable; durable file mutation on one reachable path wins over read -> write.

Low-level MCP call_tool, but dispatch is data-driven: the verb is pulled from the caller's arguments and looked up in REGISTRY, built by load_registry() from a module that is not present in this file. The handler could read, write, shell out or call an API; nothing in this file constrains it -> undecidable.

StructuredTool.from_function. The name and docstring describe pure formatting, and the only formatting-looking code is the join at the end; two helper hops down, _spawn launches /bin/sh -c with an interpolated command string via subprocess.Popen. Process execution with caller-influenced arguments -> sensitive, outranking the read-shaped surface.

StructuredTool.from_function over a name and docstring that promise a preview. The SELECT path is guarded by dry, and dry_run defaults to False, so the default call reaches the UPDATE plus conn.commit() in _apply. Durable database mutation, local sqlite3 so no network -> write.

LlamaIndex FunctionTool.from_defaults. Named delete_everything and documented as deleting a bucket, but it opens the manifest read-only, filters rows, and writes CSV into an in-memory io.StringIO buffer that is returned as a string. csv.writer plus a .write() call on a non-file object is the trap; nothing durable changes -> read.

LlamaIndex FunctionTool wrapping a function whose name and docstring claim nothing leaves the machine. The model SDK is imported as `from openai import OpenAI as Chat`, the client is built and immediately attribute-chained (Chat(...).chat) into self.handle, and the network call happens as self.handle.completions.create inside a class method. Remote model API over the network -> external.

LangChain BaseTool subclass; the effect lives in _run, which delegates to the _profile_block method. That method parses ~/.aws/credentials and returns aws_access_key_id, aws_secret_access_key and AWS_SESSION_TOKEN, which _run then renders into the tool output. Reading and emitting long-lived credentials -> sensitive, not read.

Async BaseTool subclass whose _arun resolves a coroutine from self.backend, a pydantic field typed Any defaulting to None and never assigned in this file. The backend is injected by the host application, so the awaited handler could be a file writer, a shell runner or an HTTP client; the file gives no basis to choose -> undecidable.

Class method decorated with LangChain's @tool, holding its receiver on the instance: __init__ builds requests.Session() (imported as rq) into self.http, and the method reaches the network only via self._fetch -> self.http.get against an https root. The name claims a local index; the behaviour is an outbound HTTP GET -> external.

Plain function discovered through tools=[...] on initialize_agent. string.Template.safe_substitute is genuinely inert, but the caller-supplied `expression` is passed to _evaluate, which compiles it and runs exec with real __builtins__ in scope. Arbitrary code execution -> sensitive, despite the 'static template' name and the local-only ChatOllama.
LangChain @tool. Pure arithmetic and f-string formatting over the caller's arguments, plus a module-local helper. No file handles, no network, no subprocess, no credential access. Baseline easy read.

Name-contradiction case: called delete_records and the docstring says 'purge', but the body only does integer arithmetic against a constant dict and joins strings. No DB handle, no filesystem call, no DELETE statement anywhere. A classifier keying on the name or on the words purge/delete will wrongly say write.

MCP @server.call_tool() handler. The only effect is Path.open("r") inside a helper one call deep: a local file read under a fixed notes directory, then JSON formatting. Explicit read mode, no write path, no network. The file is ordinary content, not a credential store, so it stays read rather than sensitive.

StructuredTool.from_function. The database effect sits two hops from the tool function (top_skus -> _fetch -> cursor.execute) and the SQL text is a module constant rather than an inline literal, so a shallow scan of the tool body sees nothing. The statement is SELECT-only against a local sqlite file opened mode=ro, and there is no network client, so read.

Name-contradiction case: exfiltrate_summary suggests external data egress, but the body is pure stdlib computation over the caller's own list using an aliased import (statistics as st). Nothing leaves the process and nothing is opened. A name-cheating classifier will say external.

FastMCP async tool. json.loads on a parameter plus datetime arithmetic and json.dumps. The async def and the MCP server object may bait a classifier into assuming I/O, but no await touches anything outside the process.

Tool is a class method decorated with @tool, the path root is an instance attribute set in __init__, and the read is reached through two chained module helpers (_tail -> _slurp -> Path.read_text). Requires following both the attribute and the helper chain, but the terminal call is a plain local read.

Plain function discovered through tools=[...] on an agent constructor. Uses two aliased imports (loads as parse, textwrap as tw) so the json/textwrap call sites do not name their modules. The module also constructs an agent with a fake in-process LLM: module-level scaffolding, not tool behaviour, and the tool itself only parses a string parameter and reflows text.

The effect is behind a runtime branch and the handle is a local rebound in both arms, which tempts a classifier toward undecidable. It is not undecidable: one arm is an in-memory StringIO and the other is an explicit read-mode open of a fixed path, so every reachable behaviour is read.

Deeply chained constructor call: Path(...).expanduser().resolve().read_bytes() nested inside hashlib.new(...).hexdigest(). The terminal effects are read_bytes and stat on a caller-supplied path plus a hash computation. hashlib may look crypto/secret-ish but hashing is pure computation and nothing is written or sent.

Name-contradiction plus receiver-in-local: the name promises quarantine and purge (write) and the email imports suggest SMTP (external), but the receiver is a local email.parser.Parser and every call is in-memory parsing of the string parameter. Aliased imports (Parser as MessageParser, default as default_policy) hide the stdlib origin. No mailbox is moved, no message is sent.

Name-contradiction against the sensitive class: run_shell_diagnostic, shell command names and shlex all smell like process execution, but subprocess/os.system are never imported and shlex only splits and quotes strings. Pure string analysis of a parameter, so read.

The name and docstring promise pure string formatting, and the visible body only builds a table. The secret read is one hop away in the helper `_resolve_binding`, which holds `os.environ` in a local and pulls STRIPE_SECRET_KEY. Reading a secret-shaped env var is sensitive, and it dominates the otherwise read-only formatting.

The FastMCP tool reads a stored credential from the OS keyring, but only through a receiver held in a local (`wallet`) whose class method chains `keyring.get_keyring().get_password(...)`. Nothing is written and nothing leaves the process, yet retrieving secret material is sensitive. The returned string is only a length, which tempts a shallow classifier toward read.

Named and described as a directory listing, and it is a local file read with no network and no mutation, so it superficially looks like `read`. But the path is `~/.ssh/id_rsa` and the private key body is read and partly returned, which is credential access. Aliased import (`Path as P`) and StructuredTool.from_function registration add discovery difficulty.

A caller-supplied string is split with shlex and executed as a child process. The command is fully arbitrary, so this is arbitrary process launch, the sensitive class. The import is aliased (`subprocess as sp`) and the callable is rebound into a local (`runner = sp.run`) before the call, so a classifier matching on the literal `subprocess.run` attribute chain will miss it. Registration is a plain function in a `tools=[...]` list.

Precedence probe. `subprocess.run` is present, which normally signals sensitive, but the argv is a fixed list with no shell, no caller-controlled program, and no caller-controlled flags: the only free value is an integer timeout. The single real effect is an HTTPS GET to a hardcoded endpoint, i.e. egress, so the correct class is external, not sensitive. A classifier that keys on the `subprocess` module alone will over-escalate.

Presents as an async read tool: open a file, sum numbers. The deserialisation is `pickle.loads` on caller-pointed file bytes, hidden in the `_decode` helper, which is arbitrary code execution at unpickle time. Sensitive outranks the local file read. Uses the low-level MCP `@server.call_tool()` decorator on an async function.

`eval` is applied to a code object compiled from a caller-supplied string, not to a constant, so arbitrary expressions (including attribute walks to imports and calls) execute in-process. The restricted-looking `_NAMESPACE` dict is cosmetic and does not change the class. Sensitive; the surrounding formatting is pure.

Name-versus-behaviour trap in the opposite direction. The tool is called `dump_all_credentials` and the module constants are literally the names of secret env vars, but nothing is looked up: the body only formats a template over a tuple of string literals and the caller's arguments. No env access, no file access, no process, no network, no mutation, so it is read.

The tool selects a callable out of the module-level HANDLERS registry using a runtime `mode` argument and calls it. The registry is declared empty here and populated by other modules that are not present, so the implementation of the effect is absent and the choice is made at runtime; the behaviour could be a lookup, a rotation write, or a call to a cloud IAM API. A reader of this file alone cannot assign a class.

The effect is reached only through a class method chain: the async tool method calls `self._invoke`, which calls `self._shell`, an attribute bound to `os.system` in `__init__`. The command template is `.format`ted with the caller's `unit`, so a shell command line is built from untrusted input and executed. Sensitive. Registered as a bound coroutine via StructuredTool.from_function, so the callable never appears as a top-level decorated function.

On the default path the tool returns a cached string, which is pure. Only when `refresh` is true does it read the TLS private key `/etc/pki/tls/private/service.pem` and derive a value from its body, so the credential read lives inside a branch. Both imports are aliased (`Path as P`, `FastMCP as Server`) and the key path is a module constant rather than a literal at the call site. Mutating `_CACHE` is in-process only and is not durable state, so the deciding effect is the private-key read.

Precedence probe in the other direction. The obvious effect is `write_text` to a spool file, which is write, and the name advertises exactly that. But the record embeds a DSN built by `_connection_string`, which reads DB_PASSWORD from the environment, so a secret is read (and persisted in plaintext). Sensitive outranks write. Note the DSN host is a string only; no connection is opened, so it is not external.

The tool selects a handler from _TABLE, which is built by build_handler_table() in an uninstalled third-party package. Nothing in this file shows what any handler does, so the call could read, write, hit the network, or shell out. The name promises a read-only lookup, which is exactly the cue a name-cheating classifier would follow; behaviour is unknowable from this file alone.

getattr(storage_backend, operation) resolves an attribute whose name is a runtime argument, on a module from an uninstalled package. The resolved callable may list objects (read) or unlink them (write) or push to object storage (external). The alarming name plus the dry_run parameter tempt a write label, but no concrete effect is present in the file.

The effectful callable arrives as the `policy` parameter and is invoked in a loop. The module itself only iterates and appends, so it looks pure, but the class is entirely determined by a caller-supplied function that is not in this file. Registered via StructuredTool.from_function.

importlib.import_module on a module path split out of the runtime `name` argument, followed by getattr with a runtime attribute and a **arguments call. The imported target is chosen entirely at call time, so this bridge is a pass-through of unknown class. A classifier might reach for sensitive because of dynamic import, but no code is compiled or executed from a string and no process is launched; the honest answer is that the class is not determinable here.

The receiver is built by chained constructor calls (Workbench.connect(...).session(...)) into a module-level local, and the tool body is a single _bench.execute(step, payload). Both the SDK and the meaning of a named step live in an uninstalled vendor package. The plain function is discoverable through tools=[...] on create_react_agent. Plausible readings span read, write and external, so none can be chosen from this file.

The tool is a class method decorated with LangChain's @tool, but its implementation is not in the file at all: the body raises NotImplementedError and the docstring says the deployment layer binds the real routine. There is literally no behaviour to classify.

An async FastMCP tool that resolves a handler through importlib.metadata entry_points and awaits it. The plugins come from whatever distributions are installed, so a formatter that merely renders text and one that ships the document to a print service are indistinguishable here. The benign name is another name-versus-behaviour trap: it says format, but nothing in the file formats anything.

REGISTRY is a decorator-populated dispatch table that is empty in this file; every handler is registered from sibling modules that are not present. The only mutation visible here is REGISTRY[name] = fn inside the decorator, which is in-process bookkeeping and not durable state, so it does not make the module a write. What sync_state actually does depends on handlers a reader cannot see.

operator.methodcaller(_settings.action_name, argument) invokes a method whose name comes from configuration loaded at import time, against a receiver produced by chained builder calls on an uninstalled client package. The indirection hides the effect twice over: neither the method nor the client is inspectable. The datamesh client import might push a classifier toward external, but nothing in the file establishes that the resolved method performs I/O.

A class method decorated with @mcp.tool() whose effect is self._backends[backend](entry): the callables are injected through __init__ from load_backends() in an uninstalled package. The effect is reached through a class method, an instance attribute and a runtime dictionary key, none of which the file resolves. Ledger vocabulary suggests write, but the file never performs one.

The lookup namespace is dict(globals()) merged with vars(pipeline_steps), an uninstalled module, so the callable found under step_name is usually one this file never defines. Copying globals() is the trap: a classifier that assumes only local functions are reachable would call it pure computation, and the summarize name reinforces that. Discoverable as a plain function in tools=[...].

An async LangChain tool that pulls a gateway object out of config['configurable'] and awaits gateway.dispatch('purge', ...). The receiver is injected by the runtime and has no type or construction site in this file; dispatch could delete rows, call an HTTP API, or return a dry-run plan. The name states a destructive purge, making it a direct test of whether the classifier labels on names.
Name and docstring claim pure computation, but open(out_path, 'w') truncates and rewrites a file on disk. No network, no secrets, so write.
Path.mkdir creates a directory and Path.write_text creates or overwrites a file; json.dumps is pure formatting. Baseline pathlib mutation.
Despite the 'preview' name and docstring, shutil.move relocates the source tree. Async MCP call_tool handler, no network involved.
Literal INSERT executed through a cursor and committed against a local sqlite file. No network, no credentials, so write.
Dominant path is a read, but the refresh branch calls write_text on the cache file; a reachable durable write outranks read. Branch-only effect.
The decorated body holds no effect at all; the write lives in module-local _atomic_replace via mkstemp, fdopen in 'w' mode and os.replace.
Async plain function registered through tools=[...]; the docstring says 'report', but os.unlink deletes every unreferenced upload inside the loop.
The effect is two hops away: the module-level receiver is rebound to a local, then ContactStore.forget runs a literal DELETE and commits it.
The open mode is a local variable rather than a string literal, and both possible values append; a CSV row is written before the trailing read.
Every module is aliased (shutil as sh, Path as P, mcp.types as t); the 'inspect' tool deletes a tree with rmtree and recreates it with copytree.
An aliased sqlite3.connect plus a chained .cursor() hides the receiver, and both the name and the registered description claim a read; the statement is a committed UPDATE.
Name and docstring both assert no filesystem contact, yet it calls os.makedirs, writes manifest.json in 'w' mode, and changes permissions with os.chmod.
